issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette: Vikram remembered the road before he could ever find the words. When the state convoys rolled through his homeland, they did not ask for names; they simply seized men at dusk and dragged them toward unmarked ditches. He had fled with his wife, and decades later built a quiet life as a naturalized American, but the sudden violence left no coherent narrative, only disconnected pieces that refused to fit together. Over the years, those fragmented memories refused to stay in the past. When a delivery truck backfired down his street, the auditory shock of the car sound would instantly pull him back to those headlights. The memory of that flight did not merely return; it dictated his present. Fearing that the past would consume him, he began to constantly scan his surroundings for signs of threat, pacing the perimeter of his pottery studio, watching the driveway, and steering clear of any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, as if joy would only make the sudden return of those flashes more devastating. Encountering these triggers quickly fractured his sense of self. When a police cruiser idled near his studio gate, the authority presence would send his heart hammering against his ribs, reinforcing his belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. The constant vigilance he felt necessary to survive those years now made him hypersensitive to every siren and every funeral he passed on his daily walks. He was certain that if he relaxed his guard, he would be utterly unable to cope with even the slightest upset. This low coping belief, in turn, magnified the threat of every ordinary stimulus; because he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, even the distant wail of a hearse or the sight of a neighbor's memorial service became unbearable warnings of imminent capture. The cycle tightened as the months turned into years. His conviction that he could not cope forced his mind back to the fragmented, vivid memories of the road, as if the only way to survive the present anxiety was to prepare for the old danger. In response, his avoidance habits only deepened his sense of incompetence. By routinely avoiding conflict with his wife whenever she gently suggested they visit a community center, and by constantly checking the locks and the street outside his workspace, he inadvertently proved to himself that he was helpless without his routines. This avoidance of positive events and interpersonal friction made him increasingly reactive to authority figures and car noises, which then cemented his negative appraisals of his own fragility. He was trapped in a corridor of his own making. Now, at seventy-five, Vikram sat on his workshop stool, his hands stained with dry clay, watching his wife fold laundry in the adjacent room. The silence of the house felt heavier than any threat he had known. He had finally agreed to come see a therapist after his daughter insisted his withdrawal was no longer just age or caution. He sat hoping for relief from the exhausting perimeter checks, but his deepest fear was that the diagnosis itself would confirm his worst suspicion: that he was permanently broken. He did not want to be a patient; he wanted, above all, to prove that he could still manage the quiet life they had fought so hard to build.
